lessons.title: Choosing the exam: ten complaints, ten answers
lessons.body:
## The exam is a hypothesis test, not a ritual

After the primary survey you have limited minutes and one pair of hands. The secondary exam exists to answer a narrow question: of the two or three things that could kill this particular patient, which one is this? Palpating everything on everybody feels thorough and wastes the time that actually matters.

Two questions pick the exam for you. Can this patient reliably tell you where the problem is? And could the problem be somewhere nobody is pointing? A reliable patient with one complaint gets a **focused exam**. An unreliable patient, or a complaint that could start anywhere, gets the **rapid full-body exam**.

## Unreliable means one of these five

- Altered mental status from any cause
- Alcohol or drugs on board
- A distracting injury that owns all of their attention
- A language barrier you cannot bridge in the moment
- Age extremes, because the very young and the very old under-report

## Ten complaints and the exam each one earns

| Complaint | What you examine | What you are ruling out |
|---|---|---|
| Chest pain | skin, lung sounds at 4 points, neck veins, a pulse in both arms, calves | heart attack, clot in the lung, torn aorta |
| Shortness of breath | speech length, accessory muscles, lung sounds, neck veins, ankles, SpO2 | asthma or COPD, heart failure, pneumonia |
| Abdominal pain | 4 quadrants with the painful one last, skin, pulse, last oral intake, pregnancy question in any female age 10 to 55 | bleeding aneurysm, ectopic pregnancy, obstruction |
| Headache | mental status, pupils, facial droop and arm drift and speech, neck stiffness, blood pressure | bleed in the brain, stroke, meningitis |
| Passing out (syncope) | orientation now, pulse rate and regularity, blood pressure, glucose, plus a head-to-toe for what they hit on the way down | dysrhythmia, internal bleeding, low sugar, head injury |
| Generalized weakness | glucose, temperature, skin, orientation, stroke screen, back and skin folds | sepsis, low sugar, anemia, silent heart attack |
| Altered mental status | glucose, pupils, breathing pattern, temperature, full-body sweep for trauma | the whole AEIOU-TIPS list |
| Back pain | pulses in both feet, gentle abdominal palpation for a pulsating mass, leg strength and sensation, bladder control | aneurysm, spinal cord compression |
| Fever | temperature, skin exposed for rash, mental status, lung sounds, recent antibiotics | sepsis, meningitis |
| Isolated limb injury | the joint above and the joint below, pulse-motor-sensation before and after splinting | vessel or nerve injury |

## Same complaint, different exam

A 22-year-old with chest pain that started while bench pressing, reproducible when you press on the sternum, gets a focused chest wall exam. A 72-year-old diabetic with the same words, who is gray and sweaty, gets lung sounds, both arm pulses, neck veins, legs, and a fast trip. The complaint is a doorway, not a destination.

> **Key:** Pick the exam from the worst thing the complaint could be, not from the most likely thing it is.

> **Trap:** A focused exam on an unreliable patient is how fractured pelvises and stab wounds get missed. When in doubt, go full body; it costs 90 seconds.

> **On the exam:** Vignettes that mention alcohol, a head injury, or a distracting fracture are signaling that the patient is an unreliable reporter and the answer is the rapid full-body exam.
keyPoints: Focused exam for a reliable patient with a localized complaint; rapid full-body for anyone unreliable or diffuse.
Unreliable equals altered, intoxicated, distracted by pain, language-barriered, or at an age extreme.
Choose what you palpate from the worst diagnosis the complaint could represent.
Any female age 10 to 55 with abdominal pain gets a pregnancy question.
Limb injuries get pulse, motor, and sensation checked above and below, before and after splinting.

checks.q: A 35-year-old fell off a ladder, smells strongly of alcohol, and says only his wrist hurts. Which exam?
choices: Focused exam of the wrist only
Rapid full-body exam
No exam, just splint and transport
Focused exam of the wrist and shoulder
checks.why: Alcohol makes him an unreliable reporter and the fall is a mechanism that can injure anywhere. Full body.

checks.q: Which complaint most requires you to check pulses in both feet and palpate gently for a pulsating abdominal mass?
choices: Headache
Fever
Back pain in an older adult
Isolated ankle injury
checks.why: New back pain in an older adult can be a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm, which shows as unequal or weak leg pulses and a pulsatile mass.

checks.q: Why does a syncope patient get a head-to-toe in addition to the focused cardiac assessment?
choices: Because syncope is always cardiac
Because they fell and may be injured from the fall
Because it is required for billing
Because syncope patients cannot give history
checks.why: A patient who loses consciousness hits something on the way down, and head or neck injury can be silent at first.

lessons.title: Assessment at the extremes of age
lessons.body:
## Old and young break the rules you just learned

The assessment skeleton does not change, but the normal values, the way disease shows itself, and who gives you the history all change hard at both ends of life.

## The older adult

Aging blunts every warning system. The heart cannot speed up the way a young heart does, especially on a beta blocker, so a septic 84-year-old may sit at a pulse of `78` while circling the drain. Baroreceptors are slow, so blood pressure drops without warning. Pain perception fades, so up to one third of heart attacks in people over 75 arrive as weakness, confusion, or a fall rather than chest pain. Temperature regulation fails, so serious infection often comes with a normal or low temperature.

Baseline is the whole game. "Confused" means nothing until you ask the family or the aide what this person was like yesterday. New confusion in an older adult (delirium) is an acute medical emergency, most often infection, low oxygen, low sugar, a medication, or a bleed. Long-standing confusion (dementia) is not.

Practical adjustments:

- Expect polypharmacy. Ten or more medications is common; blood thinners such as apixaban, rivaroxaban, or warfarin turn a minor head strike into a potential bleed.
- Anticipate a low-energy mechanism doing real damage. A ground-level fall in someone over 65 is a **significant mechanism**, and hip and spine fractures happen at forces a 25-year-old would shrug off.
- Undress carefully but completely. Pressure sores, an infected foot, a distended bladder, and abdominal bruising all hide under clothing.
- Respect hearing and vision. Face them, speak low-pitched and slow, do not shout, and use their hearing aids and glasses instead of talking louder.

> **Trap:** "She just has dementia" is the geriatric version of "just drunk." Any change from baseline is a finding until something explains it.

## The child

Children compensate beautifully until they do not. Cardiac arrest in kids is usually the end of a respiratory problem, not a sudden cardiac event, so breathing gets the attention.

Start across the room with the **pediatric assessment triangle (PAT)**, which needs no stethoscope and takes seconds:

1. **Appearance:** tone, interactivity, consolability, gaze, speech or cry. A floppy, unfocused, inconsolable infant is sick.
2. **Work of breathing:** nasal flaring, head bobbing, grunting, retractions, abnormal sounds.
3. **Circulation to skin:** pallor, mottling, cyanosis.

Normal vitals by age, the numbers worth memorizing:

| Age | Heart rate | Respiratory rate | Lowest acceptable systolic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Newborn to 1 year | 100 to 160 | 30 to 60 | 60 |
| 1 to 3 years | 90 to 150 | 24 to 40 | 70 |
| 3 to 5 years | 80 to 140 | 22 to 34 | 75 |
| 6 to 12 years | 70 to 120 | 18 to 30 | 80 |
| 13 and up | 60 to 100 | 12 to 20 | 90 |

A quick floor for children 1 to 10 years: systolic of `70 + (2 x age in years)`.

Technique changes too. Examine toe-to-head in toddlers so the scary parts come last, keep a stable child on the parent's lap, and read the parent, because "he is not acting right" from someone who knows the child is a vital sign. Grunting, a child too quiet to protest an exam, and a heart rate that is dropping rather than rising are all late, bad signs.

> **Key:** In children, bradycardia is not a rhythm problem; it is usually hypoxia, and the fix is oxygen and ventilation.

> **On shift:** In the emergency department the triage nurse forms the pediatric assessment triangle in the hallway. A tech who can already say "mottled, grunting, floppy" is speeding up a resuscitation.
keyPoints: Older adults blunt every classic sign: pulse, pain, fever, and blood pressure all lie.
A ground-level fall over age 65 is a significant mechanism, especially on blood thinners.
New confusion in an older adult is delirium until proven otherwise, and it is an emergency.
The pediatric assessment triangle is appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to skin.
Minimum systolic for a child 1 to 10 years is roughly 70 plus twice the age in years; bradycardia in a child means hypoxia.

checks.q: An 84-year-old on metoprolol has a septic-looking presentation but a heart rate of 76. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The heart rate rules out sepsis
The beta blocker is blunting the expected tachycardia
The patient is compensating well
The pulse reading must be wrong
checks.why: Beta blockers and aging both prevent the compensatory tachycardia, so a normal rate does not reassure you in an older adult.

checks.q: What is the lowest acceptable systolic blood pressure for a 4-year-old?
choices: 60 mmHg
70 mmHg
78 mmHg
90 mmHg
checks.why: Using 70 plus twice the age gives 70 plus 8, about 78 mmHg. Anything below that is hypotension in a preschooler.

checks.q: A 10-month-old has a heart rate of 62 and is limp. What does the heart rate most likely represent?
choices: A normal sleeping rate
Hypoxia causing bradycardia
An athletic baseline
A vagal response to the exam
checks.why: Infants normally run 100 to 160. A rate of 62 with poor tone is late hypoxia and calls for oxygen and ventilation immediately.

lessons.title: Found down with no story: reading the scene
lessons.body:
## When the patient cannot talk, the room does

A patient with no history is not a patient with no information. It is a patient whose information is sitting on a nightstand, in a purse, on a wrist, or in the timeline of who found them and why.

The first question is not what is wrong. It is **how long have they been down**, because that single number decides whether you are thinking about a fixable few minutes or hours of muscle breakdown, pressure injury, and hypothermia. Ask whoever called: when did you last see or speak to them, and what made you check on them now?

## Three checks that reverse things in minutes

1. **Glucose.** Below `70 mg/dL` is hypoglycemia. If they can swallow and protect their airway, oral glucose, usually `15 g` of gel. If they cannot, this is an ALS need and a reason to move.
2. **Pupils plus respiratory rate.** Pinpoint pupils with a rate under `12` is opioid overdose until proven otherwise. Where protocol allows an EMT to give it, naloxone is `4 mg` intranasal, half a device per nostril, repeated as needed. Ventilate first; naloxone does not move air.
3. **Stroke screen and last known well.** Facial droop, arm drift, slurred speech. The time they were last seen normal decides which hospital and which treatments.

## Read the body like a chart

- **Pupils:** pinpoint suggests opioids or a pontine bleed; one blown pupil suggests rising pressure inside the skull; large and dilated suggests stimulants or anticholinergic drugs.
- **Breathing pattern:** snoring is the tongue, slow and shallow is drugs, deep and fast (Kussmaul) suggests a metabolic acid problem such as diabetic ketoacidosis, and irregular alternating patterns suggest a brain injury.
- **Skin:** hot and dry with a fever suggests infection or heat stroke; cold and clammy suggests shock or low sugar; cherry red is uncommon and late in carbon monoxide poisoning.
- **Posture:** arms flexing inward or extending stiffly to pain (decorticate or decerebrate posturing) means a serious brain injury and a very low score on the Glasgow Coma Scale.
- **Hardware:** a dialysis fistula that buzzes under your fingers, an implanted port under the collarbone, an insulin pump, a medical alert bracelet, a vagus nerve stimulator scar.

## Work the scene, not just the patient

Pill bottles, and specifically how many pills should be left versus how many are; drug paraphernalia; alcohol containers; a note; a running car in a closed garage (carbon monoxide, and now the scene is unsafe for you); a space heater; a locked bathroom door; vomit near the mouth. Photograph or bring the bottles. Ask what the patient has been sick with in the last week, because vomiting and diarrhea in a person on blood pressure and diuretic medications explains a lot of collapses.

Do not skip trauma. Anyone found down gets a head-to-toe, because the fall that dropped them may be the reason they are not waking up, and a head bleed in a patient on apixaban can look exactly like a stroke.

> **Key:** Structural causes such as bleeds and strokes tend to produce asymmetric findings; metabolic causes such as sugar, drugs, and infection tend to produce symmetric findings with intact pupil reactivity.

> **Trap:** Finding one explanation stops most people from looking for a second. Naloxone that wakes a patient does not rule out the head injury they got when they went down.

> **On the exam:** "Found unresponsive, no history available" vignettes are almost always testing airway first, then glucose, then a structured search for reversible causes.
keyPoints: Down time is the first question; it changes everything about the risk profile.
Glucose, pupils with respiratory rate, and a stroke screen are the three fast reversible checks.
Pupils, breathing pattern, skin, posture, and implanted hardware are history you can collect without words.
Asymmetric findings point structural; symmetric findings point metabolic.
One explanation does not exclude a second, and every found-down patient gets a trauma sweep.

checks.q: An unresponsive 30-year-old has pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6. What comes first?
choices: Naloxone 4 mg intranasal
Bag-valve-mask ventilation
Blood glucose check
Rapid head-to-toe exam
checks.why: Ventilation fixes the thing that is killing them right now. Naloxone follows, but it does not move air by itself.

checks.q: Which finding most suggests a structural brain problem rather than a metabolic cause?
choices: Symmetric pinpoint pupils
Cool clammy skin
One dilated unreactive pupil with arm weakness on one side
Deep rapid breathing
checks.why: Asymmetry, meaning a unilateral blown pupil with one-sided weakness, points to rising pressure or a bleed. Symmetric findings point metabolic.

checks.q: Why is the caller's answer to 'what made you check on them now' so valuable?
choices: It establishes billing information
It helps estimate down time and the events before collapse
It identifies next of kin
It satisfies the consent requirement
checks.why: It brackets how long the patient has been down and often reveals the preceding illness, argument, or missed appointment that explains the collapse.

lessons.title: Multi-system trauma: the first ten minutes
lessons.body:
## One patient, several things trying to kill them, no time

Multi-system trauma means the forces hit more than one body region, so there is no single injury to focus on. The sequence you were taught still works, but it has to run at speed and with jobs divided, or it turns into three people doing the same thing while nobody holds the head.

The reason for the hurry is the **trauma triad of death**: bleeding causes cold, cold stops blood from clotting, poor clotting causes more bleeding, and acid builds up in between. The only real fix for internal bleeding is a surgeon. Everything you do is a delaying action.

## Assign jobs out loud before you touch anyone

With two providers, the standard split is one at the head and one at the body. The head provider holds manual in-line stabilization, owns the airway, and talks to the patient. The body provider runs XABCDE with their hands, controls bleeding, exposes, and takes vitals. Say it out loud: "I have the head and airway, you have the body." Ambiguity is what costs the minutes.

## The order under pressure

1. **Stop the bleeding you can see.** Direct pressure, then a tourniquet `2` to `3` inches above a limb wound if pressure fails, tightened until bleeding stops, time written down. Junctional wounds at the groin, armpit, or neck get packed with gauze and hard pressure.
2. **Open the airway with a jaw thrust** and suction no longer than `10` seconds at a time.
3. **Expose the chest and look, feel, listen.** An open chest wound gets a vented or three-sided occlusive dressing. Absent breath sounds on one side with rising difficulty, distended neck veins, and falling pressure is a tension pneumothorax, which an EMT cannot decompress but must recognize and call out for ALS.
4. **Circulation.** Radial pulse present or not, skin, capillary refill. Rapid weak pulse with cool pale skin is shock until proven otherwise.
5. **Disability.** AVPU, pupils, and movement in all four limbs, captured now so the hospital can compare later.
6. **Expose fully, then cover.** Cut clothing, do the sweep, then blankets and heat. Warm is a treatment, not a comfort measure.

## Package and move

Target scene time for critical trauma is `10` minutes or less, and the clock starts when you reach the patient, not when you leave. Splint fractures en route, not on scene, unless the limb is pulseless. The secondary exam happens in the truck. Call the trauma alert early so the team is standing in the bay when you arrive, and say the mechanism, the vitals, and the interventions, not a story.

> **Key:** In multi-system trauma, the assessment is not paused for treatment of anything except bleeding and airway. Everything else is done moving.

> **Trap:** A traction splint on a mid-shaft femur is right, but not before a tourniquet on the arterial bleed above it. Priorities are in XABCDE order, not in order of how dramatic the injury looks.

> **On the exam:** Questions that offer "complete the detailed physical exam on scene" as an option for a critical trauma patient are testing whether you will trade minutes for completeness. You will not.
keyPoints: Multi-system trauma needs spoken role assignment: one provider on head and airway, one on body and bleeding.
The trauma triad of death is bleeding, hypothermia, and poor clotting feeding each other.
Sequence is bleeding, airway with jaw thrust, chest, circulation, disability, expose then cover.
Scene time target is 10 minutes or less from patient contact; the secondary exam happens en route.
Warming the patient is a clotting intervention, not a comfort measure.

checks.q: A trauma patient has an arterial bleed at the upper arm and a deformed femur. What is done first?
choices: Traction splint to the femur
Tourniquet to the upper arm
Full spinal immobilization
Complete set of vital signs
checks.why: Exsanguinating hemorrhage is the X in XABCDE and comes before the airway, the splint, and everything else.

checks.q: Why is keeping a trauma patient warm considered a treatment?
choices: It prevents shivering discomfort
Cold blood clots poorly, which worsens bleeding
It raises blood pressure directly
It reduces the need for oxygen
checks.why: Hypothermia impairs the clotting cascade, which is one leg of the trauma triad of death along with bleeding and acidosis.

checks.q: When does the scene-time clock start for the 10-minute critical trauma benchmark?
choices: At dispatch
At arrival on scene at the curb
At patient contact
When the patient is loaded
checks.why: The benchmark is measured from reaching the patient to leaving the scene, so time spent walking in does not buy you extra minutes.

lessons.title: When the second set of vitals changes the plan
lessons.body:
## Reassessment is where mistakes get caught

The first set of vitals is a photograph. The second set is the movie, and the movie is what tells you what the body is doing about the problem. Below are four drills. In each one nothing about the patient's complaint changed; only the numbers did, and every plan changed with them.

## Drill 1: the reassuring blood pressure

A 24-year-old fell from a roof. First set: HR `96`, BP `126/78`, RR `18`, skin warm. Ten minutes later: HR `124`, BP `118/96`, RR `24`, skin cool and pale.

The systolic barely moved, but the diastolic climbed, so the **pulse pressure** (systolic minus diastolic) narrowed from `48` to `22`. That is clamping down, which is exactly what compensated shock looks like. Plan change: upgrade priority, request ALS, go now. Do not wait for the systolic to fall, because when it does, the compensation has already failed.

## Drill 2: the treatment that worked, briefly

A 68-year-old with COPD gets albuterol. Before: RR `32`, SpO2 `88%`, loud wheezes, speaking three words at a time. After: RR `26`, SpO2 `93%`, still wheezing but full sentences.

That is improvement and it is documented as such. Ten minutes later: RR `34`, SpO2 `89%`, and the wheezing is now faint. Quieter is worse here, because moving less air makes less noise. Plan change: prepare to assist ventilations with a bag-valve mask and tell the receiving hospital the trend, not just the current number.

## Drill 3: the improving numbers that are not

A 42-year-old with a gastrointestinal bleed. First set: HR `128`, BP `88/60`. After positioning and oxygen: HR `132`, BP `84/58`. Twenty minutes later: HR `88`, BP `76/50`, skin gray, patient sleepy.

The heart rate fell and the number looks better, but the pressure kept dropping and the mental status declined. A falling heart rate in a bleeding patient with a falling pressure is not recovery; it is the pump giving up. Plan change: this is a peri-arrest patient. Notify early and be ready for CPR.

## Drill 4: the head injury that quiets down

A 30-year-old struck in the head, initially agitated and combative. First: HR `104`, BP `138/82`. Thirty minutes later: awake but sluggish, HR `54`, BP `196/90`, breathing irregular.

Rising blood pressure, falling pulse, and irregular breathing is **Cushing's triad**, the body's late response to rising pressure inside the skull. Plan change: this is a surgical emergency. Keep the head elevated `30` degrees if there is no spinal contraindication, ventilate at a normal rate (do not hyperventilate unless signs of herniation and protocol allow), and go to a trauma center.

> **Key:** Read pairs of numbers, not single numbers. Rate against pressure, pressure against mental status, and treatment against response.

> **On the exam:** Three sets of vitals in a stem are never decoration. The direction they move is the answer.

> **On shift:** The reassessment you did not do is the one the hospital asks about. Timestamp every set, including the set taken right after each intervention.
keyPoints: A narrowing pulse pressure is compensated shock, even when the systolic looks fine.
Quieter lung sounds after a wheezing patient worsens means less air movement, not improvement.
A falling heart rate with a falling blood pressure in a bleeding patient is decompensation, not recovery.
Cushing's triad is rising blood pressure, falling pulse, and irregular breathing from rising intracranial pressure.
Vitals are interpreted in pairs and in sequence, and every set gets a timestamp.

checks.q: Vitals move from 126/78 to 118/96 with a heart rate rising from 96 to 124. What does the narrowed pulse pressure indicate?
choices: Improving perfusion
Compensated shock
Normal variation with anxiety
Medication effect
checks.why: Vasoconstriction raises the diastolic and narrows pulse pressure while the heart speeds up. That is compensated shock before the systolic falls.

checks.q: An asthmatic's wheezing becomes much fainter while respiratory rate climbs and SpO2 falls. What does this mean?
choices: The albuterol is working
Air movement is decreasing and respiratory failure is near
The stethoscope placement is wrong
The patient is calming down
checks.why: Wheeze requires airflow. A silent chest in a deteriorating asthmatic is an ominous sign that demands assisted ventilation.

checks.q: Which combination defines Cushing's triad?
choices: Low BP, fast pulse, fast breathing
High BP, slow pulse, irregular breathing
Low BP, slow pulse, deep breathing
High BP, fast pulse, shallow breathing
checks.why: Rising intracranial pressure produces hypertension, bradycardia, and an irregular respiratory pattern. It is a late and dangerous finding.

lessons.title: Difficult historians: getting the story anyway
lessons.body:
## The history is still there, you just have to change tools

Some patients cannot give you a clean story, and the reason they cannot is itself diagnostic information. Your job shifts from asking questions to gathering evidence.

## The intoxicated patient

Alcohol makes people unreliable about pain, timing, and events, and it masks head injury, low sugar, and hypothermia. Keep questions short, concrete, and repeated: "Where does it hurt? Point for me." Re-ask later, because answers change as the level changes.

Treat the exam as primary evidence, since what they tell you is secondary. Always check a glucose. Always do a full sweep for injury. Document your own observations rather than conclusions: write "odor of an alcoholic beverage, slurred speech, unsteady gait" rather than "drunk," because the first is what you saw and the second is a diagnosis you cannot make.

> **Trap:** Intoxication does not automatically remove capacity to refuse, and it does not automatically preserve it either. The test is whether they can explain back the risks in their own words.

## The aphasic or stroke patient

Aphasia comes in two flavors that matter at the bedside. In **expressive aphasia** the patient understands you but cannot get words out; they know they are wrong and get frustrated. In **receptive aphasia** the patient speaks fluently but the words are wrong, and they do not know it. Do not mistake either one for confusion or intoxication.

Use yes-or-no questions, and confirm with a second channel: "Squeeze my hand once for yes." Write questions if they can read. Give them extra time; interrupting a patient with expressive aphasia resets the whole attempt. Ask family for the last known well time, which matters more than any other fact you can collect.

## The hostile or agitated patient

Agitation is a symptom. Low oxygen, low sugar, head injury, pain, stimulants, and withdrawal all present as hostility before they present as anything else.

Stand at an angle rather than squared up, keep two arms' length, keep your exit behind you, and put one person in charge of talking. Lower your voice instead of raising it. Offer concrete choices, because choice restores control: "You can sit on the stretcher or the bench." Do not argue with a delusion and do not agree with it; redirect to the body. If you are in danger, leave and stage for police.

## The frightened child

A crying child who fights your exam is usually a reassuring finding. Get low, examine toe to head, keep the child on the parent's lap, and let the child hold the stethoscope first. Use the parent's own language: ask the child to "show me where the owie is." Never promise that something will not hurt, because the moment it does you lose every future answer.

## When nobody can tell you

Go to secondary sources: family, caregivers, the group home log, the medication list on the fridge, a prescription bottle's fill date, a pharmacy label, the nursing facility transfer packet. In New Jersey the facility must send paperwork with the patient; ask for the face sheet and the medication administration record, and take them with you.

> **Key:** When the patient is an unreliable narrator, shift weight from what they say to what you see and what the scene documents.
keyPoints: Document observations, not conclusions: slurred speech and odor, not the word drunk.
Expressive aphasia understands but cannot speak; receptive aphasia speaks fluently but wrong.
Agitation is a symptom; rule out hypoxia, hypoglycemia, head injury, and withdrawal.
For frightened children, examine toe to head on a parent's lap and never promise no pain.
Secondary sources include family, facility face sheets, medication lists, and pill bottle fill dates.

checks.q: A 70-year-old speaks in fluent but nonsensical sentences and does not seem to notice. Best description?
choices: Intoxication
Receptive aphasia
Expressive aphasia
Dementia
checks.why: Fluent speech with wrong content and no awareness of the error is receptive aphasia, a stroke finding, not confusion or intoxication.

checks.q: Which chart entry is written correctly for an intoxicated-appearing patient?
choices: Patient was drunk and uncooperative
Odor of an alcoholic beverage, slurred speech, unsteady gait, declined blood glucose
Patient was clearly abusing alcohol again
Intoxicated, refused everything
checks.why: Charting observable findings is defensible; charting the conclusion 'drunk' states a diagnosis you cannot make and reads as judgment.

checks.q: An agitated 25-year-old is shouting at your crew. What is the best first move?
choices: Have everyone speak at once to be heard
Designate one speaker, lower your voice, and offer concrete choices
Immediately restrain the patient
Tell the patient to calm down repeatedly
checks.why: One voice, a calm tone, and real choices reduce escalation. Multiple speakers and commands to calm down predictably make agitation worse.

lessons.title: Handing off an assessment the next team can use
lessons.body:
## Your assessment is only worth what survives the handoff

Everything you found dies at the door unless it moves into the next provider's head and onto the chart. The receiving team has one question: what do I need to do in the next five minutes, and why?

## The verbal handoff

The structure that works under noise is short and in a fixed order, so the listener knows what is coming next.

1. **Who and what:** age, sex, chief complaint in their words.
2. **What happened:** mechanism or onset, with a time.
3. **What you found:** the primary survey result and the pertinent positives and negatives, not everything you examined.
4. **Vitals:** first set and most recent set, with times, so the trend is audible.
5. **What you did and what it did:** every intervention with the response.
6. **What you are worried about:** the one sentence that makes the listener's plan.

Trauma teams use **MIST**: Mechanism, Injuries found, Signs including vitals, Treatment given. Hospitals often use **SBAR**: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. Same material, different container.

Give the report once, to the person who will own the patient, with the room quiet enough to hear it. Stop transferring the patient to the bed while you talk; do one at a time.

## Writing the assessment down

The narrative has to let a stranger reconstruct what you saw. Three rules make that happen.

- **Time-stamp everything.** Contact time, first vitals, each intervention, each reassessment, and the response. "Improved" with no clock attached proves nothing.
- **Write findings, not labels.** "Right pupil `5 mm` and sluggish, left `3 mm` and brisk" beats "pupils abnormal." "Speaks in three-word sentences" beats "respiratory distress."
- **Record pertinent negatives.** "Denies chest pain, no midline spinal tenderness, no incontinence, moves all four extremities" proves you asked and looked. Absence of documentation is read later as absence of assessment.

Document the things you did not do and why, too: exam limited by patient combativeness, unable to obtain blood pressure due to bilateral arm injuries, refused glucose check. Gaps that are explained are findings; gaps that are silent look like negligence.

## What the receiving team actually needs

The emergency department cannot re-create your scene. The information only you have is: the position you found them in, the down time, what the scene looked like, what the family said in the hallway, the first set of vitals, and how the patient responded to the first treatment. Lead with those, because everything else can be re-measured.

> **Key:** Say and write the trend, not just the last number. A blood pressure of `108/70` means one thing after `150/90` and something very different after `86/50`.

> **On shift:** As an emergency department tech you will be on the receiving end. Write down the first set of vitals and the down time while the crew is still talking; those two facts disappear the fastest.

> **Trap:** Do not editorialize in the chart. "Patient was noncompliant and rude" is an opinion that will be read aloud in a deposition. "Patient declined the cardiac monitor after risks were explained" is a fact.
keyPoints: Handoff order: who and what, what happened, what you found, vitals with times, what you did and its effect, what worries you.
MIST for trauma, SBAR for hospital handoffs; same content, different container.
Time-stamp every vital, intervention, and reassessment, or the trend is unprovable.
Write observable findings and pertinent negatives instead of labels and conclusions.
The facts only you have are position found, down time, scene, first vitals, and response to first treatment.

checks.q: Which piece of information is most valuable to the receiving team because they cannot obtain it themselves?
choices: The patient's current heart rate
The position the patient was found in and the estimated down time
The patient's height
The current oxygen saturation
checks.why: Vitals can be re-measured at the bedside; scene findings and down time exist only in your report and disappear if you do not say them.

checks.q: Which narrative line is written correctly?
choices: Patient in obvious distress and being difficult
Patient speaks in 3-word sentences, uses accessory muscles, SpO2 89% at 1412
Patient looked bad on arrival
Patient was hypoxic and uncooperative
checks.why: It gives observable findings with a value and a timestamp. The others are labels or opinions a reader cannot reconstruct.

checks.q: You could not obtain a blood pressure because both arms were injured. What should the chart say?
choices: Nothing, leave the field blank
BP unobtainable due to bilateral upper extremity injuries; assessed radial pulse quality instead
BP 120/80 estimated
Patient refused vitals
checks.why: An explained gap is a finding. A blank field or an invented number is far worse for the patient and for you.

lessons.title: Passing the patient assessment station
lessons.body:
## The station is a performance, and the sheet is the script

The psychomotor patient assessment station does not reward good instincts that stay silent. It rewards things you say out loud in an order an evaluator can score. The exam is graded against a printed sheet, and the classic failures are the same handful every cycle.

## The critical failures that end the station

These are the items that fail you regardless of how many other points you earned.

1. **Failure to take or verbalize body substance isolation precautions.** Say "BSI, gloves and eye protection" before you approach. This is the single most common way to lose a station in the first five seconds.
2. **Failure to determine scene safety.** Say it, do not think it.
3. **Failure to assess and manage an immediate life threat when found.** If you find the bleed and keep going, you fail. Treat, then continue.
4. **Failure to provide oxygen or ventilation when indicated.** A patient breathing `6` per minute gets a bag-valve mask at `1` breath every `6` seconds, not a nasal cannula.
5. **Failure to determine the need for transport, or an excessive scene time on a critical patient.** State your transport decision out loud.
6. **Failure to manage the airway before anything else once a life threat is found.**
7. **Performing a dangerous or harmful intervention**, including moving a patient with a possible spinal injury without stabilization.

## The quiet point-losers

- Not verbalizing the number of patients or additional resources needed.
- Not stating the mechanism of injury or nature of illness.
- Skipping the spinal precautions decision entirely rather than saying yes or no and why.
- Assessing a blood pressure but never taking a second set, so no reassessment points exist.
- Forgetting the posterior body on the log roll.
- Not checking pulse, motor, and sensation in all four limbs.
- Doing a beautiful head-to-toe on a critical patient and never transporting.

## How to structure the twelve minutes

Run the same rhythm every single time, even at home in the kitchen. Size-up out loud as six separate statements. General impression and AVPU. XABCDE with the phrase "if I found this, I would treat it now." Announce the priority decision. Then history and exam in the order the patient type demands. Then baseline vitals. Then say, "I would reassess every `5` minutes because this patient is unstable." Then the verbal transport and destination decision.

Narrate constantly. The evaluator cannot award a point for an assessment they did not hear. "I am palpating the pelvis once for instability. It is stable" earns the point; silently pressing the pelvis does not.

> **Key:** Say the finding and the meaning together. "Radial pulse present, rapid and weak, skin cool and pale, this patient is in compensated shock and is a high priority for transport."

> **On the exam:** If you realize you skipped a step, say so and do it. Recovering aloud costs nothing; evaluators score the sheet, not the elegance.

> **Trap:** Candidates who are strongest clinically fail most often, because they do the right thing quickly and quietly. Speed without narration reads as omission.
keyPoints: Critical failures include missing BSI, missing scene safety, ignoring a found life threat, and excessive scene time.
Every size-up element is a separate scored point and must be verbalized.
Treat a life threat the moment you find it, then continue the survey.
State the priority and transport decisions out loud, plus the reassessment interval.
Narrate finding and meaning together, because unspoken assessment earns zero points.

checks.q: During the assessment station you find heavy arterial bleeding during the primary survey. What do you do?
choices: Note it and finish the survey first
Stop and control it immediately, then continue
Wait for the vital signs
Report it to the evaluator at the end
checks.why: Failure to manage an immediate life threat when found is a critical failure criterion, and treat-as-you-find is the core rule of the primary survey.

checks.q: Which omission is a listed critical failure rather than just a lost point?
choices: Not asking about allergies
Not verbalizing BSI precautions
Not palpating the pelvis
Not asking last oral intake
checks.why: BSI is a critical criterion. The others cost individual points but do not by themselves end the station.

checks.q: Why do clinically strong candidates sometimes fail this station?
choices: They move too slowly
They perform steps silently, so the evaluator cannot score them
They know too much detail
They ask too many history questions
checks.why: The sheet is scored on observed and verbalized actions. Efficient silent work reads as an omission to the evaluator.

cards.front: What two questions decide between a focused exam and a rapid full-body exam?
cards.back: Can the patient reliably tell you where the problem is, and could the problem be somewhere nobody is pointing? Unreliable or diffuse means full body.

cards.front: Name the five things that make a patient an unreliable reporter.
cards.back: Altered mental status, alcohol or drugs, a distracting injury, a language barrier, and age extremes (very young or very old).

cards.front: For chest pain, what five things are on your focused exam?
cards.back: Skin color and moisture, lung sounds at four points, jugular veins, a pulse in both arms, and calves for swelling.

cards.front: What question must every female age 10 to 55 with abdominal pain be asked?
cards.back: Could you be pregnant, and when was your last menstrual period. Ectopic pregnancy is a bleeding emergency that presents as abdominal pain.

cards.front: New back pain in an older adult: what are you ruling out and how?
cards.back: Abdominal aortic aneurysm. Check pulses in both feet, palpate gently for a pulsating mass, and check leg strength and sensation.

cards.front: What do you examine on a patient who passed out, beyond the cardiac assessment?
cards.back: A head-to-toe for injuries from the fall, plus glucose, orientation, pulse regularity, and blood pressure.

cards.front: Which joints do you examine for an isolated limb injury?
cards.back: The joint above and the joint below the injury, plus pulse, motor, and sensation distal to it before and after splinting.

cards.front: Why can an older adult be in shock with a heart rate of 78?
cards.back: Aging and beta blockers blunt the compensatory tachycardia, so the heart cannot speed up. A normal rate does not rule out shock.

cards.front: How often do heart attacks in people over 75 present without chest pain?
cards.back: Roughly one third present as weakness, confusion, shortness of breath, or a fall instead of chest pain.

cards.front: Why is a ground-level fall in a patient over 65 a significant mechanism?
cards.back: Fragile bone and common blood thinners mean low-energy falls produce hip fractures, spine fractures, and head bleeds.

cards.front: What is the difference between delirium and dementia, and which is an emergency?
cards.back: Delirium is new, acute confusion and is an emergency (infection, hypoxia, low sugar, medication, bleed). Dementia is long-standing and gradual.

cards.front: What are the three sides of the pediatric assessment triangle?
cards.back: Appearance (tone, interactivity, consolability, gaze, cry), work of breathing, and circulation to skin. No equipment, done from across the room.

cards.front: What is the minimum acceptable systolic blood pressure for a child aged 1 to 10?
cards.back: Roughly 70 plus twice the age in years. A 5-year-old floor is about 80 mmHg.

cards.front: What does bradycardia in a child usually mean?
cards.back: Hypoxia. Pediatric arrest is usually respiratory in origin, so the treatment is oxygen and ventilation, not a rhythm intervention.

cards.front: In what direction do you examine a toddler, and where should the child be?
cards.back: Toe to head, so the frightening parts come last, and on the parent's lap whenever the child is stable.

cards.front: What is the first question to answer on a found-down patient?
cards.back: How long have they been down. Ask the caller when they last saw the patient and what prompted them to check now.

cards.front: What three fast reversible checks do you run on an unresponsive patient with no history?
cards.back: Blood glucose, pupils paired with respiratory rate, and a stroke screen with last known well time.

cards.front: What does deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul) suggest in an unresponsive patient?
cards.back: A metabolic acid problem, classically diabetic ketoacidosis. The body is blowing off carbon dioxide to compensate.

cards.front: One dilated unreactive pupil with one-sided weakness: structural or metabolic?
cards.back: Structural. Asymmetric findings point to a bleed, tumor, or rising intracranial pressure. Symmetric findings point metabolic.

cards.front: What implanted hardware gives you history in a silent patient?
cards.back: Dialysis fistula that buzzes, a port under the collarbone, an insulin pump, a medical alert bracelet, a pacemaker, a vagus nerve stimulator scar.

cards.front: Why does naloxone waking the patient not end your assessment?
cards.back: One explanation does not exclude a second. They may still have a head injury from the collapse, low sugar, or another drug on board.

cards.front: A car is running in a closed garage with an unresponsive patient. What changes first?
cards.back: Scene safety. Carbon monoxide makes the space unsafe; the patient comes out to fresh air before assessment continues.

cards.front: What is the trauma triad of death?
cards.back: Bleeding, hypothermia, and impaired clotting (with acidosis), each worsening the others. Warming the patient interrupts the cycle.

cards.front: How do two providers split a multi-system trauma patient?
cards.back: One owns the head: manual in-line stabilization, airway, and talking. One owns the body: XABCDE, bleeding control, exposure, and vitals. Say it out loud.

cards.front: What do you do for a bleeding wound at the groin, armpit, or neck?
cards.back: Pack the wound with gauze and apply hard direct pressure. A limb tourniquet cannot be applied to these junctional sites.

cards.front: What findings suggest a tension pneumothorax, and what can an EMT do?
cards.back: Absent breath sounds on one side, worsening difficulty, distended neck veins, falling blood pressure. Recognize, ventilate, call ALS, and transport; EMTs do not decompress.

cards.front: When does the 10-minute critical trauma scene clock start?
cards.back: At patient contact, not at arrival at the curb and not at dispatch. It ends when the ambulance begins moving.

cards.front: When is a fracture splinted on scene rather than en route?
cards.back: When the limb is pulseless or must be moved for extrication. Otherwise critical trauma patients get splinted during transport.

cards.front: Why is a blanket considered a trauma intervention?
cards.back: Hypothermia impairs clotting and worsens bleeding. Covering an exposed trauma patient is treatment for one leg of the trauma triad.

cards.front: How do you calculate pulse pressure and what does narrowing mean?
cards.back: Systolic minus diastolic. Narrowing, such as 126/78 becoming 118/96, means vasoconstriction and compensated shock.

cards.front: A wheezing patient gets quieter while SpO2 falls. Better or worse?
cards.back: Worse. Wheeze needs airflow; a quiet chest means air movement has dropped. Prepare to assist ventilations.

cards.front: A bleeding patient's heart rate falls from 132 to 88 while the pressure keeps dropping. What is happening?
cards.back: Decompensation, not recovery. The heart can no longer sustain the compensatory rate. Treat as peri-arrest.

cards.front: What are the three components of Cushing's triad?
cards.back: Rising blood pressure, falling heart rate, and irregular breathing. It signals dangerously elevated intracranial pressure.

cards.front: How high do you elevate the head of a head-injured patient, and when do you not?
cards.back: About 30 degrees when there is no spinal contraindication and blood pressure allows. Flat if spinal precautions or hypotension prevent it.

cards.front: Why must every set of vitals carry a time?
cards.back: Trend is the information. Without timestamps you cannot prove direction or rate of change, and 'improved' means nothing.

cards.front: What does a single reassuring blood pressure tell you in a young trauma patient?
cards.back: Very little. Young patients maintain systolic pressure until roughly 30 percent of blood volume is gone, then fall fast.

cards.front: How should you chart an intoxicated-appearing patient?
cards.back: Observations, not conclusions: odor of an alcoholic beverage, slurred speech, unsteady gait. Never the word drunk.

cards.front: Distinguish expressive from receptive aphasia at the bedside.
cards.back: Expressive: understands you, cannot get words out, visibly frustrated. Receptive: speaks fluently but the words are wrong and they do not notice.

cards.front: How do you get answers from a patient with expressive aphasia?
cards.back: Yes-or-no questions confirmed by a second channel, such as squeeze my hand once for yes, plus extra time without interrupting.

cards.front: Name four medical causes of agitation that must be excluded.
cards.back: Hypoxia, hypoglycemia, head injury, and stimulant use or alcohol withdrawal. Pain and urinary retention also agitate older adults.

cards.front: What body positioning keeps you safe with a hostile patient?
cards.back: Stand at an angle rather than squared up, keep two arms' length, keep your exit behind you, and have only one person speak.

cards.front: Why should you never promise a child that something will not hurt?
cards.back: One broken promise ends their cooperation for the whole call and for future providers. Say what you will do instead.

cards.front: What paperwork should you request from a nursing facility patient?
cards.back: The face sheet and the medication administration record, plus any transfer form and DNR or POLST paperwork. Take them with you.

cards.front: What six pieces make up a verbal handoff, in order?
cards.back: Who and what, what happened with a time, what you found, first and latest vitals with times, what you did and its effect, and what worries you.

cards.front: What does MIST stand for in a trauma handoff?
cards.back: Mechanism, Injuries found, Signs including vital signs, Treatment given. It is the trauma container for the same content as SBAR.

cards.front: Which facts does the hospital have no way to obtain except from you?
cards.back: Position found, estimated down time, scene appearance, what family said, the first set of vitals, and the response to your first treatment.

cards.front: Rewrite 'respiratory distress' as a documented finding.
cards.back: Speaks in three-word sentences, tripod position, accessory muscle use, SpO2 89 percent on room air at 1412. Findings, not labels.

cards.front: How do you document an assessment you could not complete?
cards.back: State the limitation and the reason, then what you did instead: BP unobtainable due to bilateral arm injuries, radial pulse quality assessed.

cards.front: Why are pertinent negatives worth charting?
cards.back: They prove you asked and looked. Absence of documentation is later read as absence of assessment.

cards.front: Why should you not transfer a patient to the bed while giving report?
cards.back: Nobody hears a report during a physical move. Do one at a time so the receiving provider actually absorbs the information.

cards.front: Name four critical failure criteria on the patient assessment station.
cards.back: No BSI, no scene safety determination, failure to treat an immediate life threat when found, and excessive scene time or no transport decision.

cards.front: Why do strong clinicians fail the assessment station?
cards.back: They work quickly and silently. The sheet scores verbalized and observed actions, so unspoken assessment earns nothing.

cards.front: What should you say after palpating the pelvis during the station?
cards.back: State the action and the finding: 'Palpating the pelvis once for instability, it is stable.' The finding is the point, not the motion.

cards.front: You realize mid-station that you skipped the spinal precautions decision. What do you do?
cards.back: Say so aloud and do it. Recovering aloud costs nothing; evaluators score the sheet items, not elegance.

cards.front: Which body region is most commonly skipped during the station and why does it matter?
cards.back: The posterior body during the log roll. Posterior wounds, including penetrating ones, hide there and it is a scored item.

cards.front: What two decisions must be stated out loud to earn their points?
cards.back: The priority or transport decision, and the reassessment interval with the reason (every 5 minutes because unstable, every 15 if stable).

quiz.q: A 27-year-old is struck by a car at low speed. He is alert, oriented, smells strongly of alcohol, and insists only his left knee hurts. Which assessment is most appropriate?
choices: Focused exam of the left knee with pulse, motor, and sensation
Focused exam of both legs and the pelvis
Rapid full-body exam with spinal precautions
History only, since he is alert and oriented
quiz.why: Alcohol makes him unreliable and auto versus pedestrian is a significant mechanism, so he gets a full-body exam. A focused knee exam misses the injuries he cannot feel.

quiz.q: A 66-year-old woman has sudden severe back pain radiating to her left flank. Which focused exam finding would most change your priority?
choices: A weaker pulse in the left foot than the right with a pulsatile abdominal mass
Tenderness over the paraspinal muscles
Pain increased by bending forward
A recent history of lifting boxes
quiz.why: Unequal leg pulses with a pulsating mass suggests an abdominal aortic aneurysm, a load-and-go emergency. The other three findings point at musculoskeletal back pain.

quiz.q: A 19-year-old has lower abdominal pain and lightheadedness. Which single question most changes your working diagnosis?
choices: Have you eaten today?
Do you have a history of kidney stones?
Have you traveled recently?
Is there any chance you are pregnant, and when was your last period?
quiz.why: A ruptured ectopic pregnancy is the abdominal emergency that kills young women fastest. Every female of childbearing age with abdominal pain gets this question.

quiz.q: Which patient should receive a focused exam rather than a rapid full-body exam?
choices: A 40-year-old ejected from a rolled vehicle
A 32-year-old who cut a finger with a kitchen knife and is alert with no other complaint
A 70-year-old found confused on the floor
A 25-year-old with a femur fracture from a motorcycle crash
quiz.why: An isolated, low-energy injury in a reliable, alert patient is exactly what a focused exam is for. The other three have either a significant mechanism or an unreliable mental status.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old diabetic reports two days of generalized weakness and no other complaint. Which set of assessments is highest yield?
choices: Pupils, grip strength, and a pelvis check
Abdominal palpation and last oral intake only
Glucose, temperature, skin, orientation, and a stroke screen
Lung sounds and a splint check
quiz.why: Weakness in a diabetic is commonly sepsis, hypoglycemia, or a silent heart attack. Sugar, temperature, perfusion, mental status, and a stroke screen cover those. The other options chase unlikely causes.

quiz.q: An 82-year-old man on metoprolol and apixaban fell from standing and struck his head. He is alert with a heart rate of 72 and blood pressure of 128/76. What is the most accurate statement?
choices: Normal vitals do not reassure you; the beta blocker masks tachycardia and the blood thinner raises bleed risk
The normal heart rate rules out significant bleeding
A fall from standing is not a significant mechanism
He can be released since he is alert and oriented
quiz.why: Beta blockers blunt the tachycardic response and anticoagulants make a ground-level fall a potential intracranial bleed. Ground-level falls over age 65 are significant mechanisms.

quiz.q: A nursing home aide says an 88-year-old resident 'is not herself today.' She is oriented to person only. Records show she is normally oriented to person, place, and time. What is your interpretation?
choices: Baseline dementia, no acute finding
Acute delirium, which is a medical emergency until a cause is found
Normal aging
Depression
quiz.why: A change from a documented baseline is delirium, commonly from infection, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, medication, or a bleed. Dementia does not change over a single day.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old struck by a car has a blood pressure of 76/50. How should you interpret this?
choices: Normal for age
Slightly high for age
Acceptable because the child is talking
Hypotensive, since the floor for this age is about 82 mmHg systolic
quiz.why: Using 70 plus twice the age gives about 82 mmHg for a 6-year-old, so 76 is hypotension and a very late sign in a child. Talking does not exclude decompensated shock.

quiz.q: Across the room, a 2-year-old is limp, makes no eye contact, has nasal flaring and grunting, and is mottled. Which part of the pediatric assessment triangle is abnormal?
choices: Appearance only
Work of breathing only
All three sides
Circulation to skin only
quiz.why: Limp with no gaze is abnormal appearance, flaring and grunting is abnormal work of breathing, and mottling is abnormal circulation to skin. All three abnormal means impending respiratory failure or shock.

quiz.q: A 9-month-old with two days of vomiting now has a heart rate of 58 and poor tone. What is the priority action?
choices: Transport without intervention and monitor the rate
Open the airway and begin oxygenation and ventilation
Obtain a blood pressure before acting
Warm the infant and reassess in 5 minutes
quiz.why: Bradycardia in an infant is hypoxia until proven otherwise, and the treatment is oxygen and ventilation. Waiting for a blood pressure or a reassessment wastes the minutes that matter.

quiz.q: A 44-year-old is found unresponsive in an apartment. Which single piece of history most changes your management?
choices: How long since anyone last saw him normal
His insurance carrier
Whether he lives alone
His occupation
quiz.why: Down time drives stroke treatment windows, expected muscle breakdown, hypothermia risk, and pressure injury. The others do not change the next ten minutes.

quiz.q: An unresponsive 60-year-old has deep, rapid breathing, a fruity odor, and dry skin. Which cause best fits?
choices: Opioid overdose
Head injury with rising intracranial pressure
Hypothermia
Diabetic ketoacidosis
quiz.why: Kussmaul respirations, a fruity odor, and dehydration are classic diabetic ketoacidosis. Opioids cause slow shallow breathing with pinpoint pupils, and rising ICP causes hypertension with bradycardia.

quiz.q: You give naloxone to an unresponsive patient with pinpoint pupils and a rate of 6, and he wakes up. What must you still do?
choices: Nothing further; the cause is identified
A full head-to-toe exam and a glucose check, since he may have injured himself and may have another cause
Release him at the scene since he is now alert
Give a second dose immediately
quiz.why: One explanation does not exclude another. Patients collapse and strike their heads, and coingestants and hypoglycemia are common. Naloxone also wears off before many opioids do.

quiz.q: An unresponsive patient has a right pupil of 6 mm that does not react and a left pupil of 3 mm that reacts briskly, with weakness on the left side. What does this pattern indicate?
choices: A metabolic cause such as hypoglycemia
Opioid toxicity
A structural intracranial problem such as bleeding or rising pressure
Simple intoxication
quiz.why: Asymmetry in pupils and motor findings points to a structural lesion. Metabolic causes such as sugar, drugs, and infection almost always produce symmetric findings.

quiz.q: During multi-system trauma care, your partner starts applying a traction splint to a deformed femur while blood is pooling under the patient's arm. What should you say?
choices: Continue the splint, then find the bleeding
Obtain vitals first, then decide
Log roll now to check the back
Stop; control the bleeding first, then splint en route
quiz.why: Exsanguinating hemorrhage precedes everything in XABCDE. A splint is a limb-saving measure; hemorrhage control is a life-saving one, and the splint can happen in the truck.

quiz.q: Two EMTs arrive at a rollover with one critical patient. What should happen before hands go on the patient?
choices: Roles are assigned out loud: one owns head and airway, one owns body, bleeding, and vitals
Both providers start a head-to-toe from opposite ends
One provider obtains a full SAMPLE history
Both providers begin spinal packaging
quiz.why: Spoken role assignment prevents duplicated work and gaps such as an unheld head. The other choices all leave the critical tasks unassigned.

quiz.q: A trauma patient has absent breath sounds on the right, increasing difficulty breathing, distended neck veins, and a falling blood pressure. What is the EMT's role?
choices: Perform needle decompression at the second intercostal space
Apply a three-sided dressing to the chest wall
Recognize a likely tension pneumothorax, ventilate, request ALS, and transport immediately
Place the patient on the affected side and reassess in 15 minutes
quiz.why: Needle decompression is outside the EMT scope. Recognition, ventilation, an ALS request, and rapid transport are the correct actions; a three-sided dressing applies to an open chest wound.

quiz.q: You reach a critical trauma patient at 1402. Which departure time meets the recommended scene-time benchmark?
quiz.why: The benchmark is 10 minutes or less from patient contact, so leaving by 1412 meets it. The clock runs from contact, not from arrival at the curb.

quiz.q: Serial vitals on a 30-year-old after a fall: BP 124/72 then 120/88 then 116/98, HR 92 then 112 then 130, skin now cool. What is happening?
choices: Compensated shock with a narrowing pulse pressure
Normal post-injury anxiety
Improving perfusion as pain is controlled
A cuff size error
quiz.why: Pulse pressure narrowed from 52 to 18 with rising tachycardia and cool skin. That is vasoconstriction compensating for blood loss, not anxiety, and it precedes a systolic drop.

quiz.q: Ten minutes after albuterol, an asthmatic's wheezing is much quieter, but her respiratory rate rose from 26 to 36 and SpO2 fell from 93 to 88 percent. What is the correct interpretation and action?
choices: Improvement; continue monitoring
Anxiety; coach her breathing
Equipment failure; change the pulse oximeter probe
Worsening air movement; prepare to assist ventilations with a bag-valve mask
quiz.why: Wheezing requires airflow, so a quieting chest with worsening rate and saturation means less air is moving. This patient is heading into respiratory failure.

quiz.q: A patient with a gastrointestinal bleed had a heart rate of 130 and BP 86/58. Now the heart rate is 84, BP is 74/50, and he is difficult to rouse. What does the slower heart rate mean?
choices: He is responding to treatment
He is decompensating and approaching arrest
He has vagal stimulation from nausea
He was previously miscounted
quiz.why: A falling heart rate alongside a falling pressure and declining mental status is failure of compensation, not recovery. Treat as peri-arrest and notify the hospital.

quiz.q: A head-injured patient who was combative is now sluggish with BP 198/92, HR 50, and irregular breathing. What is the priority?
choices: Restrain him for crew safety
Hyperventilate at 30 breaths per minute
Recognize Cushing's triad, ventilate at a normal rate, elevate the head if permitted, and transport to a trauma center
Withhold oxygen to avoid raising intracranial pressure
quiz.why: This is rising intracranial pressure and a surgical emergency. Routine hyperventilation is harmful, and withholding oxygen worsens brain injury.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old speaks in long fluent sentences that make no sense and appears unaware of it. His wife says he was normal an hour ago. What is the best action?
choices: Chart confusion of unknown cause and transport routinely
Assume intoxication and check a breath alcohol level
Wait 20 minutes to see if speech clears
Recognize possible receptive aphasia, obtain last known well time, and treat as a stroke
quiz.why: Fluent but meaningless speech with no awareness is receptive aphasia, a stroke sign. Last known well time determines treatment eligibility, so any delay costs options.

quiz.q: Which narrative entry about an intoxicated-appearing patient is most defensible?
choices: Odor of an alcoholic beverage noted, speech slurred, gait unsteady, glucose 96 mg/dL
Patient was drunk and refused to cooperate
Obvious alcoholic, typical frequent flyer
Patient intoxicated, no assessment possible
quiz.why: Observable findings plus an objective value can be defended later. The other entries record a diagnosis you cannot make or an opinion that reads badly in a deposition.

quiz.q: A 23-year-old is shouting and pacing at a party. Before assuming a behavioral cause, which findings must you exclude?
choices: Dehydration and fatigue only
Anxiety disorder and caffeine intake
Hypoxia, hypoglycemia, head injury, and stimulant use or withdrawal
Recent travel and allergies
quiz.why: Agitation is a symptom with medical causes that kill. Low oxygen, low sugar, a head bleed, and drug effects must be excluded before labeling behavior as psychiatric.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old is crying, clinging to her mother, and pushing your hands away during an exam. How should you proceed?
choices: Separate her from the parent to reduce distraction
Examine her on the parent's lap, toe to head, letting her handle the stethoscope first
Restrain her briefly to complete a head-to-toe
Skip the physical exam entirely and transport
quiz.why: Vigorous protest is reassuring, and keeping the child with the parent while working toe to head preserves cooperation. Separation and restraint escalate and give you a worse exam.

quiz.q: You are handing off a patient who was found on a bathroom floor for an unknown period. Which item should lead your report because the hospital cannot obtain it?
choices: The position found, the scene appearance, and the estimated down time
The current oxygen saturation
The patient's home address
The current heart rate
quiz.why: Vitals will be repeated on arrival, but scene findings and down time exist only in your head. Leading with them changes the receiving team's plan.

quiz.q: Which handoff line best conveys the trend rather than a snapshot?
choices: Blood pressure is 108 over 70
The patient looks better now
Vitals are stable
Pressure went from 150 over 90 at 1405 to 108 over 70 at 1425 while the heart rate climbed from 88 to 122
quiz.why: Two timed sets with the direction of change tell the receiving team the patient is deteriorating. A single value or the word 'stable' hides that entirely.

quiz.q: Both of a patient's arms are fractured and no blood pressure could be obtained. What belongs in the chart?
choices: A blank blood pressure field
The reason it was unobtainable and what you assessed instead, such as radial pulse quality and capillary refill
An estimated blood pressure of 120/80
A note that the patient refused vitals
quiz.why: An explained gap is itself an assessment finding. A blank field looks like an omission and an invented number is falsification.

quiz.q: During the NREMT patient assessment station, a candidate finds spurting bleeding, states it aloud, and continues to the airway without treating it. What is the outcome?
choices: Full credit, because it was verbalized
Loss of one point only
Critical failure for not managing an immediate life threat when found
No effect if the bleeding is controlled later
quiz.why: Treat-as-you-find is the core rule, and failing to manage a discovered life threat is a listed critical failure regardless of whether it was verbalized.

quiz.q: Which behavior most improves a candidate's score on the assessment station?
choices: Narrating each action and its finding out loud as it happens
Working as quickly as possible with minimal talking
Performing a full detailed exam on every patient
Waiting until the end to summarize all findings
quiz.why: Evaluators score observed and verbalized actions. Silent efficiency reads as omission, and a full exam on a critical patient risks an excessive scene time failure.

quiz.q: A candidate completes a thorough head-to-toe on a patient with an unstable airway and hypotension, then states the patient should be transported after packaging. What is the likely result?
choices: Pass, because the exam was complete
Pass with minor deductions for slow work
Fail only if the exam missed a finding
Critical failure for excessive scene time and failure to prioritize the airway
quiz.why: Airway management and transport priority come before a detailed exam in a critical patient. Both delayed airway care and excessive scene time are listed critical criteria.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 83-year-old female, general weakness
scenarios.intro: You are dispatched at 1105 to a single-story home for an 83-year-old female with general weakness. Dispatch says she is conscious and breathing, and her daughter called. This is a low-acuity-sounding call on a busy morning. You are attending.

steps.prompt:
The house is clean and quiet. The daughter meets you at the door and says, "She just has no energy today. She takes a lot of medications. I don't think it's an emergency, I just couldn't get her out of the chair."

What is your most useful opening question?

choices.text: "What is she normally like on a good day, and what is different right now?"
choices.feedback: Correct. Baseline is the whole assessment in a geriatric patient. Without it, 'weak' and 'confused' mean nothing.

choices.text: "Does she have insurance and a primary doctor?"
choices.feedback: Administrative, not clinical. It buys you nothing in the next ten minutes.

choices.text: "Do you want us to take her in or not?"
choices.feedback: You have not assessed her yet, and this hands the medical decision to a family member who does not have your information.

steps.prompt:
The daughter says her mother normally does her own cooking and crossword puzzles, but today she has been "foggy" and did not know what day it was. The patient is in a recliner, awake, oriented to person only, skin warm and dry. Medications on the table include metoprolol, lisinopril, apixaban, and metformin.

First set of vitals is being taken. What do you specifically want, beyond the standard set?

choices.text: Blood glucose and a temperature, plus a stroke screen
choices.feedback: Correct. New confusion is delirium until proven otherwise, and sugar, infection, and stroke are the checkable causes.

choices.text: Nothing extra; her vitals are within normal limits
choices.feedback: The vitals are normal-looking, which in an 83-year-old on a beta blocker is exactly the trap. A rate of 84 may already be her maximum effort.

choices.text: A 12-lead ECG performed by your BLS crew
choices.feedback: Outside the EMT scope in most BLS systems. Request ALS if you want a monitor; do not claim a skill you do not have.

choices.text: Pupils and grip strength only
choices.feedback: Useful, but incomplete. You still need a glucose and a temperature before you can call this neurologic.

steps.prompt:
Glucose is `142 mg/dL`. Temperature is `37.2 C` orally. Stroke screen shows no droop, no arm drift, speech is slow but clear. She says her back hurts a little and she has not been drinking much. You help her stand to move to the stair chair and she becomes pale and says the room is spinning.

What do you do?

choices.text: Sit her back down immediately and repeat vitals
choices.feedback: Correct. Symptoms on standing are a finding, not an inconvenience. Sit her down and get a second set.

choices.text: Keep her moving to the chair quickly to get the call done
choices.feedback: Harmful. You are walking a possibly hypovolemic patient toward a fall.

choices.text: Reassure her it is normal to feel dizzy when standing at her age
choices.feedback: This normalizes an abnormal finding. Orthostatic symptoms in a patient who has not been drinking suggest volume loss.

steps.prompt:
Seated again, she is pale and slightly sweaty. Your partner hands you the second set of vitals and notes she is warmer to the touch than she was ten minutes ago.

How does this change your plan?

choices.text: Upgrade to a higher priority, request an ALS intercept, lay her supine with legs elevated if tolerated, keep her warm, and begin transport
choices.feedback: Correct. Fever with tachycardia, hypotension, and new confusion in an older adult is sepsis until proven otherwise, and this is now time-critical.

choices.text: Continue routine transport and recheck vitals at the hospital
choices.feedback: You just documented a decompensation and then ignored it. This is the exact failure the reassessment exists to prevent.

choices.text: Give her water to drink since she is dehydrated
choices.feedback: Do not give oral fluids to a confused patient with a declining mental status; aspiration risk is real and she may need an operating room or procedures.

choices.text: Repeat vitals in 5 minutes before making any decision
choices.feedback: Reassessment is right, but you already have enough to act. Move and reassess en route.

steps.prompt:
You are transporting. The receiving emergency department asks for a report. You have 30 seconds.

Which report is best?

choices.text: "83-year-old female, general weakness, en route, will give the rest on arrival."
choices.feedback: This tells the department nothing they can act on, and they will not have a room or a team ready.

choices.text: "83-year-old female, one day of weakness and new confusion from a baseline of fully oriented. Initial vitals 84, 118/70, temp 37.2. Now 118, 88/60, temp 38.4, respirations 26, sat 94 on oxygen. On metoprolol and apixaban. Glucose 142, no stroke signs. I am treating this as sepsis; ETA 8 minutes, she will need a bed with a team."
choices.feedback: Correct. Baseline, trend with two timed sets, the medications that matter, the negatives you checked, your concern, and a time. That builds their plan before you arrive.

choices.text: "Elderly female, weak and a little out of it, vitals soft, see you in 8."
choices.feedback: Vague adjectives instead of numbers. 'Soft' vitals could mean anything and the trend is invisible.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: in an older adult, the first set of vitals lied and the second set told the truth. A heart rate of 84 on a beta blocker, a temperature of 37.2, and a blood pressure of 118/70 all looked fine, but the baseline change her daughter described was the real finding from the first minute. Standing her up acted as a stress test and unmasked the volume loss. New confusion plus fever plus tachycardia plus hypotension in a geriatric patient is sepsis until someone proves otherwise, and the reassessment is what converted a routine transport into a time-critical one. Two habits carried this call: ask what the patient is like on a good day, and repeat vitals after any position change or intervention.

scenarios.title: Found down: unknown male in a parking garage
scenarios.intro: At 0250 you are dispatched to a parking garage for an unknown male down. A security guard found him and does not know how long he has been there. Police are en route but not on scene yet. The garage is cold and poorly lit. You have no name, no history, and nobody who knows him.

steps.prompt:
The guard points to a man lying on his side near a stairwell. No vehicles are moving. The guard says, "I walked this level around midnight and he wasn't here, but I'm not certain."

What do you do first?

choices.text: Scan the immediate area for hazards and needles, then approach with gloves and eye protection
choices.feedback: Correct. Unknown down in a public space at night means sharps, vomit, and unseen people. Safety and BSI come before the patient.

choices.text: Run to the patient and begin an assessment immediately
choices.feedback: Speed is not the same as priority. Providers get stuck with needles doing exactly this.

choices.text: Wait in the ambulance for police before entering the garage
choices.feedback: Reasonable if there were a threat, but nothing here suggests violence and delay costs a patient who may be apneic. Stay alert instead.

steps.prompt:
He does not respond to your voice. He responds to a trapezius pinch with a moan. Respirations are slow and shallow, roughly 6 per minute. Pupils are about `2 mm` bilaterally. There is a small amount of vomit near his mouth and a bruise over his right eyebrow.

What comes first?

choices.text: Administer naloxone 4 mg intranasal immediately
choices.feedback: Naloxone does not move air, and giving it into a nose full of vomit while he is hypoxic wastes the first minute. Ventilate first.

choices.text: Suction the airway, then open it with a jaw thrust and begin bag-valve-mask ventilation at 1 breath every 6 seconds
choices.feedback: Correct. The bruise means you assume a possible spinal injury, so jaw thrust rather than head-tilt, and ventilation fixes the hypoxia that is killing him now.

choices.text: Apply a non-rebreather mask at 15 liters per minute
choices.feedback: A mask delivers oxygen to a patient who is not moving enough air. At 6 breaths per minute he needs your ventilations, not just a higher concentration.

choices.text: Log roll him supine and begin a rapid head-to-toe
choices.feedback: The exam can wait 60 seconds. Airway and ventilation come first, and the roll happens with the airway controlled.

steps.prompt:
Ventilations are effective; the saturation is climbing. Your partner asks whether to give naloxone. Meanwhile you notice his jacket pocket has a pill bottle and there is a phone on the ground nearby.

What is your approach?

choices.text: Give naloxone per protocol while continuing ventilation, and collect the pill bottle as history
choices.feedback: Correct. Naloxone is given alongside ventilation, not instead of it, and the bottle is the only history available to you.

choices.text: Hold naloxone entirely because he might become combative
choices.feedback: The risk of withdrawal agitation does not outweigh reversing respiratory depression, and protocols account for it with titration.

choices.text: Stop ventilating to give naloxone, then wait to see if he breathes
choices.feedback: Harmful. Interrupting ventilation on a hypoxic patient to wait for a drug to work is the wrong order.

choices.text: Leave the bottle where it is; it is not your property
choices.feedback: Medication containers are patient history. Bring them or photograph the label; the hospital cannot go back and get it.

steps.prompt:
He begins breathing at `16` per minute and opens his eyes but is slow and confused. The bottle is a prescription for oxycodone filled six days ago, count nearly empty. Glucose reads `88 mg/dL`. He cannot tell you his name reliably.

What is your next step?

choices.text: Consider the call resolved and offer him a refusal since he is now awake
choices.feedback: Harmful. He is not oriented, naloxone wears off before oxycodone does, and he has a head strike and a temperature of 35.1 C.

choices.text: Complete a rapid head-to-toe, cover him with blankets, and continue transport with reassessment every 5 minutes
choices.feedback: Correct. One explanation does not exclude a second: he has a facial bruise, hypothermia, and an unknown down time.

choices.text: Focus only on the head injury and defer the rest of the exam to the hospital
choices.feedback: Partial. The head matters, but an unknown down time demands a full sweep for pressure injury, other trauma, and other drugs.

choices.text: Let him walk to the ambulance to save time
choices.feedback: He is confused with a possible head and spine injury. Walking him is both a fall risk and a spinal risk.

steps.prompt:
Head-to-toe shows a `4 cm` bruise above the right eyebrow, no skull depression, no fluid from ears, pupils now `4 mm` and equal, no midline neck tenderness that he can report reliably, clear lungs, soft abdomen, and a reddened area over his right hip where he was lying. He is shivering under two blankets.

Which statement best frames your report to the hospital?

choices.text: "Opioid overdose, reversed with naloxone, now fine."
choices.feedback: This closes the case prematurely and hides the head injury, the hypothermia, and the unknown down time.

choices.text: "Unknown male, found down in a garage, unwitnessed, down time up to 3 hours. Initially unresponsive to voice, respirations 6, sat 82, pinpoint pupils. Ventilated and given naloxone at 0301; now respirations 18, sat 99, GCS 14, glucose 88. Also has a forehead contusion, temp 35.4, and a pressure area on the right hip. Concerned about head injury and re-sedation as naloxone wears off."
choices.feedback: Correct. It names the down time, the before-and-after trend with a time, the reversible cause treated, and the two problems that are still open.

choices.text: "Another overdose, he's awake now, he'll probably want to sign out."
choices.feedback: Editorializing and predicting the patient's behavior. It biases the receiving team against a patient with an untreated head injury and hypothermia.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: no history is not no information. The guard's uncertain timeline set a down-time bracket, the pill bottle's fill date and remaining count was a medication history, and the bruise, the temperature, and the pressure area were all findings that the patient could never have reported. The sequence held: airway and ventilation before the drug, the drug alongside ventilation rather than instead of it, then the full sweep because one explanation never excludes a second. Naloxone wearing off before the opioid does is the reason this patient is still a transport, not a refusal, and the report that names what remains unresolved is the one that protects him after you leave.
